I cannot determine the exact infimum. The bounds established below are
\[
\boxed{\frac19\leq \inf c\leq\frac15}.
\]
In fact, the upper-bound proof produces **one fixed finite triangle-free graph** that works whenever \(\delta(G)>|G|/5\).

Both proofs below are elementary. A runnable verification script follows them.

## 1. The upper bound

A coloring is called **wide** here if the endpoints of every walk of length \(3\) have different colors. Walks may repeat vertices. Thus a wide coloring is, in particular, proper.

We repeatedly use the following observation:

> A graph with no \(C_3\) or \(C_5\) has no odd closed walk of length at most \(5\).

Indeed, deleting portions between repeated vertices from an odd closed walk produces an odd cycle no longer than the walk.

### 1.1 A wide coloring with at most 36 colors

Let \(G\) have \(n\) vertices, contain no \(C_3,C_5\), and satisfy \(\delta(G)>n/5\).

Choose a maximum-cardinality collection
\[
r_1,\ldots,r_s
\]
whose open neighborhoods \(B_i=N(r_i)\) are pairwise disjoint. Since each \(B_i\) has more than \(n/5\) vertices,
\[
s\leq4.
\]

For each vertex \(v\), define
\[
L(v)=\{i:N(v)\cap B_i\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
This set is nonempty: otherwise \(v\) could be added to the collection.

If \(uv\in E(G)\), then
\[
L(u)\cap L(v)=\varnothing. \tag{1}
\]
Otherwise, for some \(i\), choose
\(a\in N(u)\cap B_i\) and \(b\in N(v)\cap B_i\). Then
\[
u,a,r_i,b,v,u
\]
is a closed walk of length \(5\), a contradiction.

Put
\[
S_i=\{v:L(v)=\{i\}\},\qquad
K=\{v:|L(v)|\geq2\}.
\]

**Each \(S_i\) is a wide color class.**  
First, any \(v,w\in S_i\) have a common neighbor. If their neighborhoods were disjoint, replacing \(r_i\) by \(v,w\) would give a larger collection of pairwise disjoint neighborhoods: their neighborhoods avoid every \(B_j\) with \(j\ne i\).

Now a length-\(3\) walk from \(v\) to \(w\), together with their common neighbor, would give a closed walk of length \(5\). This proves the claim.

**The graph \(G[K]\) is bipartite.**  
By (1), adjacent labels are disjoint. Among subsets of a set of size at most \(4\), two disjoint subsets both having size at least \(2\) must be complementary two-element subsets. Thus edges in \(G[K]\) run only between complementary label classes. These occur in disjoint pairs, so \(G[K]\) is bipartite.

Choose a bipartition color \(\beta(v)\in\{0,1\}\) on \(K\). For \(v\in K\), also put
\[
J(v)=\{i:N(v)\cap S_i\ne\varnothing\}.
\]

Color \(G\) as follows:

* give \(S_i\) its own color;
* give \(v\in K\) the color \((\beta(v),J(v))\), using colors distinct from the \(S_i\)-colors.

There are at most
\[
s+2\cdot2^s\leq36
\]
colors.

To check wideness, suppose \(x,a,b,y\) is a length-\(3\) walk whose endpoints have the same color. Endpoints in some \(S_i\) have already been ruled out, so \(x,y\in K\).

If \(a\in S_i\), then \(i\in J(x)=J(y)\). Choose \(z\in S_i\cap N(y)\). The walk
\[
a,b,y,z
\]
contradicts wideness of \(S_i\). The case \(b\in S_i\) is symmetric. Otherwise the entire walk lies in the bipartite graph \(G[K]\), so \(\beta(x)\ne\beta(y)\), again a contradiction.

Hence the coloring is wide.

### 1.2 An explicit finite triangle-free target

For a positive integer \(m\), define \(H_m\) by
\[
V(H_m)=\{(i,A):i\in[m],\ A\subseteq[m]\setminus\{i\}\},
\]
with adjacency
\[
(i,A)\sim(j,B)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
i\in B,\quad j\in A,\quad A\cap B=\varnothing.
\]

This graph is triangle-free. In a purported triangle
\((i,A),(j,B),(k,C)\), the two edges incident with \((i,A)\) imply
\(i\in B\cap C\), contrary to the edge between \((j,B)\) and \((k,C)\).

Given a wide \(m\)-coloring \(\phi\), map
\[
v\longmapsto
\left(\phi(v),\{\phi(w):w\in N(v)\}\right).
\]
For an edge \(uv\), the two neighborhood-color sets are disjoint: a common color would give neighbors \(x\in N(u)\), \(y\in N(v)\) with
\(\phi(x)=\phi(y)\), contradicting the walk \(x,u,v,y\). Thus this map is a homomorphism to \(H_m\).

Taking \(m=36\) proves the required property for every \(c>1/5\).

---

## 2. The lower bound

We first construct graphs with arbitrarily large chromatic number but a very uniform cover by independent sets.

### 2.1 Shift graphs and their independent-set covers

For \(N\geq k\), let \(S(N,k)\) have the increasing \(k\)-tuples from \([N]\) as vertices, with edges
\[
(a_1,\ldots,a_k)(a_2,\ldots,a_{k+1})
\]
for every increasing \((k+1)\)-tuple.

For fixed \(k\), their chromatic numbers are unbounded as \(N\) grows. Indeed, a proper \(q\)-coloring \(\phi\) of \(S(N,k)\) gives a coloring of \(S(N,k-1)\) by
\[
(a_1,\ldots,a_{k-1})
\longmapsto
\{\phi(a_1,\ldots,a_{k-1},b):b>a_{k-1}\}.
\]
This is proper: for adjacent lower tuples, the color of
\((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) belongs to the first set and cannot belong to the second. Consequently,
\[
\chi(S(N,k-1))\leq2^{\chi(S(N,k))}.
\]
Since \(S(N,1)=K_N\), iteration proves the assertion.

Now let \(k\geq4\) be even. For every permutation \(\pi\) of \([N]\), define \(A_\pi\) to consist of tuples whose \(\pi\)-largest entry occurs in one of the positions
\[
3,5,\ldots,k-1.
\]

Each \(A_\pi\) is independent. To see this, consider two adjacent, overlapping windows. If both were selected, the \(\pi\)-largest entry of their union could not be the discarded first entry or the newly added last entry. It would therefore be their common maximum. Its positions in the two windows differ by one, so they cannot both be among the listed odd positions.

There are \(M=N!\) sets in this cover, counting repetitions. Every vertex belongs to exactly
\[
r=M\frac{k-2}{2k}
\]
of them, because each position is equally likely to contain its \(\pi\)-largest entry. Thus
\[
\frac rM=\frac{k-2}{2k}\longrightarrow\frac12. \tag{2}
\]

### 2.2 A dense augmentation of a subdivision

Let \(F\) be any graph with independent sets
\[
A_1,\ldots,A_M
\]
such that every vertex belongs to exactly \(r\) of them.

Orient the edges of \(F\) arbitrarily. Replace every oriented edge \(uv\) by
\[
u-x_{uv}-y_{uv}-v.
\]
Call this subdivision \(B\). Its vertices have three types, with associated labels:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{type}&\text{vertex}&\text{label}\\ \hline
U&u&u\\
X&x_{uv}&u\\
Y&y_{uv}&v
\end{array}
\]
Each type is independent.

For an integer \(W\geq1\), augment \(B\) as follows. For each type \(T\in\{U,X,Y\}\):

* introduce \(W\) pad vertices for each \(A_i\);
* join each such pad to precisely the base vertices of type \(T\) whose labels lie in \(A_i\);
* introduce \(rW\) additional vertices, each adjacent to all \(MW\) pads of that type.

There are no other new edges.

Writing
\[
b=|V(F)|+2|E(F)|,
\]
the resulting graph \(G\) satisfies
\[
|V(G)|=b+3(M+r)W,\qquad \delta(G)\geq rW. \tag{3}
\]
Every base vertex has exactly \(rW\) pad neighbors; pads have \(rW\) neighbors in their additional part; and additional vertices have degree \(MW\geq rW\).

### 2.3 Verifying that the augmentation has no \(C_3\) or \(C_5\)

Here is the relevant subdivision fact:

> If a length-\(3\) walk in \(B\) has endpoints of the same type, their labels are adjacent in \(F\).

For type \(U\), it traverses a subdivided edge. For type \(X\), its possible forms, up to reversal, are
\[
x_{uv},y_{uv},v,x_{vw}
\quad\text{or}\quad
x_{uv},u,y_{wu},x_{wu}.
\]
The endpoint labels are respectively \(u,v\) or \(u,w\), adjacent in \(F\). Type \(Y\) is symmetric.

It follows that no pad has two base neighbors joined by a length-\(3\) walk: their labels would be adjacent vertices in one independent set \(A_i\).

Now classify possible short cycles.

* **Triangles:** the base has none. A pad's base neighbors all have one independent type. An additional vertex has only pad neighbors, and pads are independent. Thus no triangle exists.
* **A \(C_5\) containing an additional vertex:** its two neighboring pads belong to the same family. The remaining length-\(3\) path between those pads would have to use an edge between base vertices of that same type, or an edge between pads. Neither exists.
* **A \(C_5\) with no additional vertices:** it contains at most two pads.
  * With no pads, it lies in \(B\), whose cycles have length at least \(9\).
  * With one pad, the other four edges give a forbidden length-\(3\) base path between two of its neighbors.
  * With two pads, their common base neighbor forces them to have the same type. The remaining base edge would then join two vertices of that type, impossible.

Therefore \(G\) contains neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\).

### 2.4 Why this obstructs every fixed triangle-free target

Let \(H\) be finite and triangle-free, and put \(h=\max(1,|V(H)|)\).

Choose an even \(k\geq4\), and then choose \(N\) large enough that
\[
\chi(F)>h,\qquad F=S(N,k).
\]
Use the independent-set cover from Section 2.1.

If \(G\to H\), then every original edge \(uv\) of \(F\) gives a length-\(3\) walk in \(H\) from the image of \(u\) to the image of \(v\). Those images cannot coincide: a closed walk of length \(3\) in a simple graph gives a triangle. Thus the images of the original vertices constitute a proper \(|V(H)|\)-coloring of \(F\), a contradiction.

Finally, (2) and (3) give
\[
\lim_{W\to\infty}\frac{rW}{b+3(M+r)W}
=\frac{r}{3(M+r)}
=\frac{k-2}{3(3k-2)}
\longrightarrow\frac19.
\]
For any \(c<1/9\), choose even \(k\) so that the middle expression exceeds \(c\), then choose \(W\) sufficiently large. Explicitly, it suffices to take
\[
W>\frac{cb}{r-3c(M+r)}.
\]
The resulting \(G\) has \(\delta(G)\geq c|V(G)|\) and does not map to \(H\).

This proves the lower bound.

---

## 3. Executable checks

The proof above covers arbitrary sizes. The following script additionally performs actual finite checks:

* all applicable unlabeled graphs through seven vertices;
* symbolic impossibility of a triangle in the full target \(H_{36}\);
* all permutations in four shift-cover examples;
* the subdivision-walk lemma for all **760 oriented graphs on at most four vertices**;

## 1. The upper bound

A coloring is called **wide** here if the endpoints of every walk of length \(3\) have different colors. Walks may repeat vertices. Thus a wide coloring is, in particular, proper.

We repeatedly use the following observation:

> A graph with no \(C_3\) or \(C_5\) has no odd closed walk of length at most \(5\).

Indeed, deleting portions between repeated vertices from an odd closed walk produces an odd cycle no longer than the walk.

### 1.1 A wide coloring with at most 36 colors

Let \(G\) have \(n\) vertices, contain no \(C_3,C_5\), and satisfy \(\delta(G)>n/5\).

Choose a maximum-cardinality collection
\[
r_1,\ldots,r_s
\]
whose open neighborhoods \(B_i=N(r_i)\) are pairwise disjoint. Since each \(B_i\) has more than \(n/5\) vertices,
\[
s\leq4.
\]

For each vertex \(v\), define
\[
L(v)=\{i:N(v)\cap B_i\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
This set is nonempty: otherwise \(v\) could be added to the collection.

If \(uv\in E(G)\), then
\[
L(u)\cap L(v)=\varnothing. \tag{1}
\]
Otherwise, for some \(i\), choose
\(a\in N(u)\cap B_i\) and \(b\in N(v)\cap B_i\). Then
\[
u,a,r_i,b,v,u
\]
is a closed walk of length \(5\), a contradiction.

Put
\[
S_i=\{v:L(v)=\{i\}\},\qquad
K=\{v:|L(v)|\geq2\}.
\]

**Each \(S_i\) is a wide color class.**  
First, any \(v,w\in S_i\) have a common neighbor. If their neighborhoods were disjoint, replacing \(r_i\) by \(v,w\) would give a larger collection of pairwise disjoint neighborhoods: their neighborhoods avoid every \(B_j\) with \(j\ne i\).

Now a length-\(3\) walk from \(v\) to \(w\), together with their common neighbor, would give a closed walk of length \(5\). This proves the claim.

**The graph \(G[K]\) is bipartite.**  
By (1), adjacent labels are disjoint. Among subsets of a set of size at most \(4\), two disjoint subsets both having size at least \(2\) must be complementary two-element subsets. Thus edges in \(G[K]\) run only between complementary label classes. These occur in disjoint pairs, so \(G[K]\) is bipartite.

Choose a bipartition color \(\beta(v)\in\{0,1\}\) on \(K\). For \(v\in K\), also put
\[
J(v)=\{i:N(v)\cap S_i\ne\varnothing\}.
\]

Color \(G\) as follows:

* give \(S_i\) its own color;
* give \(v\in K\) the color \((\beta(v),J(v))\), using colors distinct from the \(S_i\)-colors.

There are at most
\[
s+2\cdot2^s\leq36
\]
colors.

To check wideness, suppose \(x,a,b,y\) is a length-\(3\) walk whose endpoints have the same color. Endpoints in some \(S_i\) have already been ruled out, so \(x,y\in K\).

If \(a\in S_i\), then \(i\in J(x)=J(y)\). Choose \(z\in S_i\cap N(y)\). The walk
\[
a,b,y,z
\]
contradicts wideness of \(S_i\). The case \(b\in S_i\) is symmetric. Otherwise the entire walk lies in the bipartite graph \(G[K]\), so \(\beta(x)\ne\beta(y)\), again a contradiction.

Hence the coloring is wide.

### 1.2 An explicit finite triangle-free target

For a positive integer \(m\), define \(H_m\) by
\[
V(H_m)=\{(i,A):i\in[m],\ A\subseteq[m]\setminus\{i\}\},
\]
with adjacency
\[
(i,A)\sim(j,B)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
i\in B,\quad j\in A,\quad A\cap B=\varnothing.
\]

This graph is triangle-free. In a purported triangle
\((i,A),(j,B),(k,C)\), the two edges incident with \((i,A)\) imply
\(i\in B\cap C\), contrary to the edge between \((j,B)\) and \((k,C)\).

Given a wide \(m\)-coloring \(\phi\), map
\[
v\longmapsto
\left(\phi(v),\{\phi(w):w\in N(v)\}\right).
\]
For an edge \(uv\), the two neighborhood-color sets are disjoint: a common color would give neighbors \(x\in N(u)\), \(y\in N(v)\) with
\(\phi(x)=\phi(y)\), contradicting the walk \(x,u,v,y\). Thus this map is a homomorphism to \(H_m\).

Taking \(m=36\) proves the required property for every \(c>1/5\).

## 2. The lower bound

We first construct graphs with arbitrarily large chromatic number but a very uniform cover by independent sets.

### 2.1 Shift graphs and their independent-set covers

For \(N\geq k\), let \(S(N,k)\) have the increasing \(k\)-tuples from \([N]\) as vertices, with edges
\[
(a_1,\ldots,a_k)(a_2,\ldots,a_{k+1})
\]
for every increasing \((k+1)\)-tuple.

For fixed \(k\), their chromatic numbers are unbounded as \(N\) grows. Indeed, a proper \(q\)-coloring \(\phi\) of \(S(N,k)\) gives a coloring of \(S(N,k-1)\) by
\[
(a_1,\ldots,a_{k-1})
\longmapsto
\{\phi(a_1,\ldots,a_{k-1},b):b>a_{k-1}\}.
\]
This is proper: for adjacent lower tuples, the color of
\((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) belongs to the first set and cannot belong to the second. Consequently,
\[
\chi(S(N,k-1))\leq2^{\chi(S(N,k))}.
\]
Since \(S(N,1)=K_N\), iteration proves the assertion.

Now let \(k\geq4\) be even. For every permutation \(\pi\) of \([N]\), define \(A_\pi\) to consist of tuples whose \(\pi\)-largest entry occurs in one of the positions
\[
3,5,\ldots,k-1.
\]

Each \(A_\pi\) is independent. To see this, consider two adjacent, overlapping windows. If both were selected, the \(\pi\)-largest entry of their union could not be the discarded first entry or the newly added last entry. It would therefore be their common maximum. Its positions in the two windows differ by one, so they cannot both be among the listed odd positions.

There are \(M=N!\) sets in this cover, counting repetitions. Every vertex belongs to exactly
\[
r=M\frac{k-2}{2k}
\]
of them, because each position is equally likely to contain its \(\pi\)-largest entry. Thus
\[
\frac rM=\frac{k-2}{2k}\longrightarrow\frac12. \tag{2}
\]

### 2.2 A dense augmentation of a subdivision

Let \(F\) be any graph with independent sets
\[
A_1,\ldots,A_M
\]
such that every vertex belongs to exactly \(r\) of them.

Orient the edges of \(F\) arbitrarily. Replace every oriented edge \(uv\) by
\[
u-x_{uv}-y_{uv}-v.
\]
Call this subdivision \(B\). Its vertices have three types, with associated labels:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{type}&\text{vertex}&\text{label}\\ \hline
U&u&u\\
X&x_{uv}&u\\
Y&y_{uv}&v
\end{array}
\]
Each type is independent.

For an integer \(W\geq1\), augment \(B\) as follows. For each type \(T\in\{U,X,Y\}\):

* introduce \(W\) pad vertices for each \(A_i\);
* join each such pad to precisely the base vertices of type \(T\) whose labels lie in \(A_i\);
* introduce \(rW\) additional vertices, each adjacent to all \(MW\) pads of that type.

There are no other new edges.

Writing
\[
b=|V(F)|+2|E(F)|,
\]
the resulting graph \(G\) satisfies
\[
|V(G)|=b+3(M+r)W,\qquad \delta(G)\geq rW. \tag{3}
\]
Every base vertex has exactly \(rW\) pad neighbors; pads have \(rW\) neighbors in their additional part; and additional vertices have degree \(MW\geq rW\).

### 2.3 Verifying that the augmentation has no \(C_3\) or \(C_5\)

Here is the relevant subdivision fact:

> If a length-\(3\) walk in \(B\) has endpoints of the same type, their labels are adjacent in \(F\).

For type \(U\), it traverses a subdivided edge. For type \(X\), its possible forms, up to reversal, are
\[
x_{uv},y_{uv},v,x_{vw}
\quad\text{or}\quad
x_{uv},u,y_{wu},x_{wu}.
\]
The endpoint labels are respectively \(u,v\) or \(u,w\), adjacent in \(F\). Type \(Y\) is symmetric.

It follows that no pad has two base neighbors joined by a length-\(3\) walk: their labels would be adjacent vertices in one independent set \(A_i\).

Now classify possible short cycles.

* **Triangles:** the base has none. A pad's base neighbors all have one independent type. An additional vertex has only pad neighbors, and pads are independent. Thus no triangle exists.
* **A \(C_5\) containing an additional vertex:** its two neighboring pads belong to the same family. The remaining length-\(3\) path between those pads would have to use an edge between base vertices of that same type, or an edge between pads. Neither exists.
* **A \(C_5\) with no additional vertices:** it contains at most two pads.
  * With no pads, it lies in \(B\), whose cycles have length at least \(9\).
  * With one pad, the other four edges give a forbidden length-\(3\) base path between two of its neighbors.
  * With two pads, their common base neighbor forces them to have the same type. The remaining base edge would then join two vertices of that type, impossible.

Therefore \(G\) contains neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\).

### 2.4 Why this obstructs every fixed triangle-free target

Let \(H\) be finite and triangle-free, and put \(h=\max(1,|V(H)|)\).

Choose an even \(k\geq4\), and then choose \(N\) large enough that
\[
\chi(F)>h,\qquad F=S(N,k).
\]
Use the independent-set cover from Section 2.1.

If \(G\to H\), then every original edge \(uv\) of \(F\) gives a length-\(3\) walk in \(H\) from the image of \(u\) to the image of \(v\). Those images cannot coincide: a closed walk of length \(3\) in a simple graph gives a triangle. Thus the images of the original vertices constitute a proper \(|V(H)|\)-coloring of \(F\), a contradiction.

Finally, (2) and (3) give
\[
\lim_{W\to\infty}\frac{rW}{b+3(M+r)W}
=\frac{r}{3(M+r)}
=\frac{k-2}{3(3k-2)}
\longrightarrow\frac19.
\]
For any \(c<1/9\), choose even \(k\) so that the middle expression exceeds \(c\), then choose \(W\) sufficiently large. Explicitly, it suffices to take
\[
W>\frac{cb}{r-3c(M+r)}.
\]
The resulting \(G\) has \(\delta(G)\geq c|V(G)|\) and does not map to \(H\).

This proves the lower bound.

            (C for C in it.combinations(V, size)
             if all(not N[a] & N[b]
                    for a, b in it.combinations(C, 2))),
